uncited: This family of methods addresses the fundamental limitation of vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the production of "floating" volumetric ellipsoids that lack an explicit, watertight geometric boundary .

By aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors (such as SDFs, depth maps, or explicit meshes), these methods enforce positional and normal consistency to enable accurate mesh extraction, physically-based rendering, and robust initialization .

Unlike sibling methods that may rely solely on photometric loss or implicit constraints, this family explicitly integrates geometric supervision into the training or post-processing pipeline to ensure the Gaussians conform to physical surfaces .
All methods in this family share the goal of aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior.
The core mechanism involves adding geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss $\mathcal{L}_{rgb}$.
**Positional Consistency:** Gaussian centers $\mathbf{c}_i$ are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates.
**Normal Consistency:** The orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior.
where $\mathcal{L}_{geo}$ is the geometric consistency loss and $\mathcal{L}_{norm}$ is the normal consistency loss .
The weights $\lambda_{geo}$ and $\lambda_{norm}$ are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy .
The concept of aligning Gaussian representations with geometric priors emerged as a solution to the lack of explicit geometry in 3D Gaussian Splatting.
While 3DGS excels at novel view synthesis, its volumetric nature makes mesh extraction difficult .
Early works like [SuGaR](9191-sugar.md) introduced post-hoc regularization to flatten Gaussians into surfels .

Subsequent methods like [Geo-Splatting](9201-geo-splatting.md) integrated explicit meshes for physically-based rendering , while others like [GeoCE Loss](17334-geoce-loss.md) focused on feature-space geometric consistency .
The family continues to evolve with methods addressing initialization  and sparse-view constraints .
